title: JEE Maths Formula Revision: How to Memorise Every Formula (Without Rote) + Free Quiz
meta_title: JEE Maths Formula Revision: Memorise Every Formula
meta_desc: A method for JEE maths formula revision that beats rote: active recall, spaced repetition, one-page sheets and a final-months schedule. Free quiz.
excerpt: Most JEE aspirants copy 300 formulas into a register and forget half by exam day. Here is the recall-based method I would use instead — plus a quick quiz to test your formula memory.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
A student I coached in Kota once showed me his formula register — 180 pages, colour-coded, genuinely beautiful. Then I asked him for the formula for the sum of the first n terms of a GP. He froze. He had copied every formula and recalled almost none. That gap is the whole problem with JEE maths formula revision, and it is why the ‘write it all out neatly’ approach quietly fails thousands of aspirants every year.

The fix is not more copying. It is changing what you do with the formulas after you have written them. Below is the method I trust, built on how memory actually works, with a revision schedule for the final months and a chapter-priority list so you spend your hours where the marks are.

Why rote memorisation fails for JEE

Rote gives you a formula you can read but not retrieve under pressure. In the exam hall your brain is loaded — timer running, adrenaline high — and a passively-copied formula simply is not there. Worse, JEE rarely asks you to state a formula. It asks you to choose the right one from twenty you half-know and apply it in a twisted problem. Passive reading trains recognition; the exam demands recall and selection. Those are different skills.

There is also the volume trap. Across Algebra, Calculus, Coordinate Geometry, Trigonometry and Vectors, you are looking at roughly 300–350 standard results. Re-reading a 180-page register for the tenth time feels like work but moves almost nothing into long-term memory.

Active recall: test, do not re-read

Active recall means closing the book and forcing your brain to produce the formula from nothing. It is uncomfortable, which is exactly why it works — the effort of retrieval is what builds the memory.

  • Write the formula name or a trigger (e.g. ‘sum of GP’, ‘derivative of arctan’) on one side of a card, the formula on the back.
  • Look at the trigger, say the formula out loud before flipping.
  • Got it wrong or hesitated? That card goes back into the deck for sooner review.

In my experience this single switch — from re-reading to self-testing — is the highest-leverage change most JEE students can make. Ten minutes of recall beats an hour of passive revision.

Spaced repetition: review just before you forget

Memory fades on a predictable curve. Spaced repetition schedules each review at the moment you are about to forget, which resets the curve and stretches the interval each time. A workable, low-tech schedule for a new formula:

ReviewWhenWhat you do
1stSame dayRecall from the trigger card
2ndNext dayRecall + solve one problem using it
3rdAfter 3 daysRecall only
4thAfter 1 weekRecall + a mixed-topic question
5thAfter 3 weeksRecall; if solid, retire the card

Apps like Anki automate this, but honestly a shoebox of index cards and three labelled dividers (‘daily’, ‘weekly’, ‘monthly’) does the same job. The tool matters far less than the discipline.

Build a one-page formula sheet per chapter

For every chapter, condense everything onto a single A4 sheet. The constraint is the point — forcing 40 results onto one page makes you decide what is core and how the results connect. A good sheet has the formula, a one-line trigger for when to use it, and a tiny worked example.

These sheets become your last-week revision. On the morning of a mock, you should be able to flip through all of Calculus in fifteen minutes. If your sheet cannot do that, it is too crowded — cut the derivations, keep the results.

Derive, do not memorise, the ones you can

Some formulas should never be memorised because deriving them takes ten seconds and the derivation itself is unforgettable. A few I always tell students to derive rather than store:

  • sin 2θ and cos 2θ — drop straight out of the sum formulas.
  • Sum of a GP — the S − rS trick reconstructs it every time.
  • Sum of squares / cubes — recognise the pattern instead of storing three separate results.

The counter-intuitive bit: aiming to derive fewer formulas but understanding them deeply beats memorising all 300 shallowly. A formula you can rebuild is one you can never truly forget.

Chapter priority: revise where the marks are

Not every chapter earns equal revision time. Based on the weight these areas carry across recent JEE Main and Advanced papers, front-load your recall practice like this:

PriorityChaptersWhy
HighCalculus, Coordinate Geometry, Algebra (Sequences, Binomial)Largest, most predictable share of questions
MediumTrigonometry, Vectors & 3D, ProbabilityFormula-heavy, quick marks once memorised
LowerComplex Numbers, Matrices & DeterminantsFewer questions, but easy scorers

Your revision schedule for the final months

In the last 8–10 weeks, formula work should be daily and short, not marathon sessions. A pattern that holds up: 20 minutes of card recall each morning across two chapters, one full-length or half-length mock every 2–3 days, and a Sunday where you revise only the cards you got wrong that week. That error deck is gold — it is a personalised map of exactly what your memory drops under pressure.

One honest caveat: do not start a brand-new memorisation system in the final fortnight. If cards are not already a habit, switch to just your one-page sheets and heavy problem-solving. Consistency you have built beats a perfect system you cannot maintain.

Test your formula recall now

Below is a free 8-question quiz on the exact formulas that show up most in JEE maths — calculus, sequences, binomial, trigonometry and coordinate geometry. Try it under a one-minute-per-question limit to mimic real recall. When you want every formula in one clean, exam-ready place, the JEE formula book linked below collects them chapter by chapter with triggers and examples.

quiz.title: JEE Maths Formula Recall Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight formula-recall questions across calculus, algebra, trigonometry and coordinate geometry. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.

questions.q: The derivative of tan x with respect to x is:
questions.explanation: d/dx (tan x) = sec² x. It is worth pairing this with d/dx (cot x) = −cosec² x on the same card.

questions.q: The sum of the first n natural numbers, 1 + 2 + … + n, equals:
questions.explanation: 1 + 2 + … + n = n(n + 1)/2. Derive it by pairing the first and last terms rather than memorising blindly.

questions.q: In an arithmetic progression with first term a and common difference d, the nth term is:
questions.explanation: The nth term of an AP is a + (n − 1)d, because you add d exactly (n − 1) times after the first term.

questions.q: How many terms are there in the binomial expansion of (a + b)ⁿ?
questions.explanation: (a + b)ⁿ expands into n + 1 terms, with exponents running from n down to 0.
sin 2θ = 2 sin θ cos θ. The other three options are all forms of cos 2θ — a classic trap.

questions.q: The discriminant of the quadratic ax² + bx + c = 0 is:
questions.explanation: The discriminant is b² − 4ac; its sign tells you whether the roots are real and distinct, real and equal, or complex.

questions.q: The eccentricity of a circle is:
questions.explanation: A circle has eccentricity 0. For a parabola it is 1, for an ellipse 0 < e < 1, and for a hyperbola e > 1.

questions.q: The magnitude of the vector 3i + 4j is:
questions.explanation: |3i + 4j| = √(3² + 4²) = √25 = 5. This is just the distance formula applied to a position vector.

faq.q: How many formulas do I actually need to memorise for JEE maths?
faq.a: Roughly 300 to 350 standard results across all chapters, but a good chunk of those can be derived on the spot rather than stored. Aim to truly recall the high-frequency ones from Calculus, Coordinate Geometry and Algebra first.

faq.q: Is it better to derive or memorise JEE formulas?
faq.a: Both. Memorise results you use constantly and cannot quickly rebuild, but derive anything whose derivation is short and memorable — sin 2θ, sum of a GP, sum of squares. A formula you can reconstruct is one you never fully lose.

faq.q: How do I stop forgetting formulas right before the exam?
faq.a: Use spaced repetition, not last-minute cramming. Review each formula on an expanding schedule — same day, next day, after three days, after a week — and keep an error deck of the ones you keep missing so revision targets your real weak spots.

faq.q: When should I start formula revision for JEE?
faq.a: Start light recall alongside your regular study from the beginning, then intensify in the final 8 to 10 weeks with daily 20-minute card sessions and frequent mocks. Do not launch a brand-new memorisation system in the last fortnight.
